title: When things break: handling an incident calmly
summary: A simple, repeatable order for the bad day: confirm, stop the damage with a rollback or a kill switch, tell people, fix it properly, and learn from it without blame.
youWillLearn: Why you stop the damage first and look for the cause second
How a rollback and a kill switch buy you calm time
What to tell users and clients while it is still broken
How to run a short, blameless review so it does not happen again

glossary.deploy: Putting a new version of the code live. On Vercel, every deploy is kept as its own version.
glossary.incident: Any unplanned problem that hurts users right now, like an outage, a broken feature or leaked data.
glossary.severity: How bad an incident is, usually ranked: everyone blocked, some users blocked, or minor annoyance.
glossary.mitigate: Reduce the harm quickly, even before you know the cause. Rolling back is the classic example.
glossary.rollback: Putting the previous working version of the app back live, without building anything new.
glossary.kill switch: A setting that turns one feature off instantly, without a deploy, while the rest of the app keeps working.
glossary.feature flag: An on/off setting checked by the code while it runs, so a feature can be enabled or disabled without changing code.
glossary.status page: A public page that tells users what is broken and when the next update will come.
glossary.root cause: The underlying reason an incident happened, as opposed to the visible symptom.
glossary.postmortem: A short written review after an incident: what happened, why, and what will change. Blameless means it looks at systems, not at people.

steps.title: Friday evening, a normal deploy
body: Notely's users reach the app server, the computer running Notely's code, which asks the Claude API (Anthropic's AI) for summaries.
At 18:25, you made a deploy: you put a new version of Notely's code live on Vercel, the company that runs it. Everything looked fine, so you went to make dinner.

scene.caption: Users, the app server running the 18:25 version, and the Claude API. You are off duty.

steps.title: Friday, 18:40, the phone buzzes
body: An alert: summary errors for hundreds of users, starting right after the 18:25 deploy. Your heart rate jumps.
You open the code and start changing things directly on main, the live branch. Three quick fixes in ten minutes. The third breaks login as well. Panic turned one broken feature into two.
changes: ~ App Server → Claude API: summaries fail since 18:25
~ You → App Server: three rushed fixes, straight to main
~ Broken features 0 → 2: login breaks too
~ Users told No need → Nobody

scene.caption: Rushed fixes pile onto a live problem and break a second feature.

steps.title: A fixed order for bad days
body: Calm comes from having a plan before you need it. Every incident, an unplanned problem hurting users right now, follows the same order.
Confirm what is broken. Stop the damage. Tell people. Fix the cause properly. Learn from it. The key move: stopping the damage comes before understanding it.

callout.text: First aid. You stop the bleeding before you ask how the accident happened. The diagnosis comes later, in a calmer room.

changes: ~ You → App Server: the rushed fixes stop

scene.caption: You stop typing. The Incident step tile above will follow you through the five steps.

steps.title: Confirm: what broke, for whom, since when
body: Take two minutes to look before acting. Is it real? Which feature? How many users? When did it start, and what changed right before: a deploy, a setting, an outage at a provider?
Then rank its severity. Everyone locked out of their notes is the top level. Summaries and login failing for many users, as here, is serious.

callout.text: Check your providers' status pages too. If the Claude API or Supabase (Notely's database host) is down, your fix is a clear error message and patience, not a code change.

changes: ~ App Server: errors began with the 18:25 deploy
~ Incident step Normal → Confirm

scene.caption: The errors line up with the 18:25 deploy.

steps.title: Stop the damage: roll back
body: The errors started with the 18:25 deploy. The fastest way to mitigate, or reduce the harm, is a rollback: put the last good deploy, from 17:10, back live. That undoes your rushed fixes too.
Vercel keeps every deploy. Instant Rollback switches back to an older one in seconds, with nothing to build. Then you can investigate calmly.

callout.text: The bad code is still on main. Revert it there too (lesson 1). After an Instant Rollback, Vercel also stops putting new deploys live on its own, so your fix goes live only when you promote it (make it the live one).

changes: + Deploy 18:25 and Deploy 17:10: two kept versions
~ App Server runs Deploy 17:10 again
~ Broken features 2 → 0
~ Incident step Confirm → Stop harm

scene.caption: The live app points back at the 17:10 version. Summaries and login work again.

steps.title: Or switch off only one feature
body: Sometimes rolling back does not help: the bug is old, or the Claude API itself is down. Then turn off only the broken part with a kill switch.
It is a feature flag: an on/off setting the code checks on every request. Summaries pause with a friendly message, and notes keep working.

code.caption: Store the flag in the database or a flag service. On Vercel, changing an environment variable only takes effect after a new deploy.

changes: − Deploy 18:25 and Deploy 17:10
~ Claude API down, in a what-if: rollback would not help
~ App Server: kill switch on, summaries paused, notes work

scene.caption: What if the Claude API were down? Switch summaries off; the rest of Notely keeps working.

steps.title: Tell people early, then on a schedule
body: Back to the real Friday. Post a short update as soon as the problem is confirmed, on a status page (a public page about outages) or in the app. On client work, tell the client directly.
Say what is affected, what is safe, what you are doing, and when the next update comes. Then keep that promise.

code.code:
Summaries, then login, failed from 18:25.
Your notes are safe. We rolled back at 18:50,
and everything works again. We are fixing the cause.
Next update by 19:30.
code.caption: Four sentences: what broke, what is safe, what you are doing, when you will speak again.

changes: + Status Page: tells users what broke and what is safe
~ Claude API and App Server back to Friday's real state
~ Users told Nobody → 18:52
~ Incident step Stop harm → Tell users

scene.caption: You write one update; the status page carries it to every user.

steps.title: Fix it properly, on a branch
body: Now find the root cause, not only the symptom. The 18:25 deploy renamed a function, and the summary code still called it by the old name.
Fix it the normal way: a branch, a test that reproduces the bug (lesson 3), a pull request, a preview. Then put it live and watch the errors for a few minutes.

callout.text: Paste the full error and the time it started. Ask Claude Code to explain the cause before it changes code. Ask for the smallest fix, on a branch, with a test that failed before and passes after. Refuse pushes to main and unrelated cleanup.

changes: + Fix Branch: the real fix, with a test, through a pull request
~ Status Page steps back
~ Incident step Tell users → Fix

scene.caption: The proper fix goes through the normal route and replaces the rollback.

steps.title: A rollback does not roll back data
body: Rolling back swaps the code, not the database, where Notely keeps every note. Broken rows a bad deploy wrote, or a table it changed, stay.
What if the 18:25 deploy had also renamed the column body to content? The 17:10 code asks for body and crashes. Make database changes additive: add the new column, drop the old one later.

callout.text: If a change dropped or renamed a column, a rollback can make things worse. That is the case for point-in-time recovery from lesson 5, so know where your backups are before the bad day.

changes: − You, Status Page, Fix Branch: a what-if about the data
+ Database: keeps every note; the rollback never touched it
~ What if: a renamed column makes the 17:10 code crash

scene.caption: What if: old code meets a renamed column. A rollback cannot fix this.

steps.title: Learn, then recap
body: Within a few days, write a one-page postmortem: timeline, impact, root cause, two or three changes. Blameless: ask "what let this through?", not "who did it?". Here: no test covered summaries, and rushed fixes went straight to main.
The order: confirm, stop the damage, tell people, fix, learn. Code rolls back; data does not.

callout.text: For client work, a calm postmortem builds trust. Clients forgive outages. They do not forgive silence, or the same outage twice.

changes: ~ Back to the real Friday: App Server and Database healthy
~ Incident step Fix → Learn

scene.caption: Everything healthy again, and a written note of what will change.

quiz.question: Errors spiked right after a deploy 15 minutes ago. You think you know which line is wrong. What do you do first?

options.text: Push a fix to main right away, since you know the line.
options.why: You think you know. If you are wrong, you have added a second untested change to a live incident.

options.text: Roll back to the previous deploy, then fix it on a branch.
options.why: Rollback restores users in seconds and gives you calm time. The fix then goes through tests and a preview like any other change.

options.text: Wait to see if the errors stop on their own.
options.why: Errors that start right after a deploy are almost always caused by it. Waiting only extends the outage.

quiz.question: The Claude API is having an outage. Summaries fail, but the rest of Notely works. What is the best move?

options.text: Roll back to last week's deploy.
options.why: Your code did not change; the provider is down. An older version calls the same failing API.

options.text: Ask Claude Code to rewrite the summary code.
options.why: Nothing is wrong with your code. Rewriting it during an outage adds risk and fixes nothing.

options.text: Turn summaries off with a kill switch, show a friendly message, post a status update.
options.why: You cannot fix their outage. You can make your app fail gracefully and keep users informed until it recovers.

quiz.question: You rolled back a deploy that also renamed the database column notes.body to notes.content. The app still crashes. Why?

options.text: The rollback did not finish. Try it again.
options.why: The rollback worked. It only changes code.

options.text: The old code expects body, but the database now has content.
options.why: Rollbacks swap code, never data. Renames should happen in steps (add the new column, copy, switch the code, drop the old one later) so old and new code both work.

options.text: Vercel's cache is serving the new code.
options.why: Instant Rollback switches the deploy directly. The mismatch is between code and database.

takeaways: Follow one order every time: confirm, stop the damage, tell people, fix, learn.
Mitigate before you investigate: a rollback or a kill switch buys calm time.
Post early updates with a promised time for the next one. Silence is worse than bad news.
Rollbacks swap code, not data. Keep database changes additive so old code still works.
Write a short, blameless postmortem with two or three concrete changes.
